title: Old Wires, Big Problem: Why U.S. Flights Stopped on Friday
summary:
On Friday afternoon, planes across the United States suddenly stopped taking off. Air traffic controllers ordered a ground stop, meaning no departures at all, for four hours, starting at 3:54 p.m. Eastern time. It was the longest such stop since the attacks of September 11, 2001.

The cause was a tech problem during an upgrade. Workers were replacing old copper telephone wires with new fibre-optic cables in the air traffic control system. The work was being done by a company called L3Harris. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said a router that was being worked on began flooding other air traffic control systems with data, cutting off communication with planes. Controllers stopped flights to stay safe while the problem was fixed.

The shutdown rippled across the country. More than 15,000 flights were delayed or cancelled that day, affecting about 1.5 million passengers. Some travellers sat stuck inside planes on the runway, unable to take off or return to the gate. On Saturday, more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and 7,000 delayed as airlines tried to clear the backlog. The Federal Aviation Administration said schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday.

Duffy said the government is still trying to work out whether the fault came from the wire replacement or from the router itself. He warned the same kind of problem could happen again unless Congress approves money to modernise air traffic control. President Donald Trump has asked for 30.1 billion dollars for the upgrades, and Duffy has previously said the system needs a 50 billion dollar overhaul.
why_it_matters: Air travel depends on old computer and wire systems, so one tech fault can stop flights across a whole country and affect millions of people.

background_read: Air traffic control is the system that guides planes safely through the sky and helps them take off and land.
Controllers talk to pilots through radio and computer links, so they need fast and steady connections to do their job.
Old copper telephone wires carry signals slowly and can wear out, while fibre-optic cables use light to send signals much faster.
If those links break, controllers may stop flights until the system is safe to use again.
